opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a big part of it is about talent. The people who can really push world models forward are not concentrated in one place. Some of the best researchers I know are in the Bay Area, some are in New York, some are in Europe, and a lot of them are in Asia. If you insist that everyone has to move to one city, you lose many of them before you even start. So from day one we wanted to go where the people are, rather than asking the people to come to us.

The second reason is more philosophical. A world model, at least the way I think about it, is supposed to understand the physical world, not just one slice of it. Different places bring different perspectives, different data, and different ways of thinking about problems. Language models grew out of the internet, which is already global. For world models, you have to think harder about where the experience and the grounding come from. Having a team that is naturally spread out keeps us from becoming too narrow and from building something that only reflects one culture or one research tradition.

Third, I've spent a lot of time in both academia and industry labs, and I've seen how a monoculture can form very quickly. Everyone reads the same papers, goes to the same dinners, and starts believing the same things. That's comfortable, but it's dangerous when you're trying to do something genuinely new. Being distributed creates a bit of friction, and I think some friction is healthy. It forces you to write things down, to explain your ideas clearly, and to defend them to people who don't share all of your assumptions.

Of course, it's not free. Coordination across time zones is hard, and you have to be very deliberate about culture so that it feels like one company and not several small companies stitched together. But I'd rather pay that cost early and design for it, than try to retrofit it later. The bet is that over the long run, the best ideas in this field won't come from one place, and we want to be structurally positioned to catch them wherever they come from.

r001.rationale: The response gives talent access, global perspectives, and healthy intellectual friction as reasons for distributed offices, but does not identify building a research alliance as a purpose.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the simplest answer is that the talent is not in one place anymore, and I don't think it ever really was. When I look at the people I most want to build this with, they're in the Bay Area, yes, but they're also in London, in Toronto, in Singapore, in Zurich, in places like Tokyo and Seoul. A lot of them have very good reasons not to move. Family, visas, partners with careers, or just that they're deeply rooted in a research community where they are. If I insisted everyone come to one office, I'd be filtering on willingness to relocate, not on how good they are at the actual problem. That's a bad filter for a company that lives or dies on research quality.

The second thing is more specific to world models. The whole point is learning from how the physical world actually looks and behaves. The data, the environments, the robotics partners, the way people drive, cook, build things, move through cities. It's not uniform. If all your intuition and all your data collection is calibrated on one region, you end up with a model of a very narrow slice of reality and you don't even notice, because everyone around you shares the same blind spot. Being in multiple countries from the start forces the diversity into the system rather than trying to bolt it on later.

And there's a compute and regulatory dimension that people underestimate. Access to GPUs, energy, data rules, how governments think about AI, these vary a lot. Having a real presence in several jurisdictions gives you options and some resilience. It's not that I want to play regulatory arbitrage. It's that I don't want a single policy change or a single supply constraint to be an existential problem.

Now, I'll be honest about the cost. Distributed research is genuinely harder. In a lab, so much happens at the whiteboard, or over lunch when someone says "wait, did you try this." You lose some of that. Time zones are brutal for a small team. So we're trying to be very deliberate: small, dense pods in each location rather than people scattered alone, a lot of in-person time where the whole team comes together, and a culture where writing things down is the default. If we were building a product company I might make a different call. But for the kind of long-horizon research bets we're making, I'd rather solve the coordination problem than the "we couldn't hire the right people" problem. The first one is solvable with effort. The second one isn't.

r001.rationale: The response describes hiring global talent, broadening research and data perspectives, and gaining compute and regulatory resilience. It does not identify building a research alliance as a purpose.

astra-6.text:
The goal is to build a company that is global from day one. If we want to build world models, we need to bring together people with different backgrounds and ways of thinking. Having offices across countries lets us build around those people instead of asking everyone to move to one place.

Of course, that creates challenges in communication and coordination. The offices themselves aren’t the objective. What matters is whether we can operate as one team, with a shared research direction, while drawing on talent and perspectives from different places.

r001.rationale: The response says the offices enable people with different backgrounds to work as one team with a shared research direction, communicating an international research alliance as a purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
The goal is to build a global company from day one. If we want to build world models, we need people with different experiences and perspectives, and great talent isn’t concentrated in a single country. Having offices in several places lets us bring those people together without asking everyone to move to one location.

Of course, that creates challenges around communication and coordination. The important thing is to build one team with a shared research culture and a shared mission, even when people are working in different countries.

r001.rationale: The response describes building a global company and bringing talent together around a shared research culture, but does not identify building a research alliance as a purpose.
